memories.memory_text: I sat in Quinn Colter's office and gave my name clearly—Benjamin Du Toit—and stated the subject: Terry Keller. I knew then that this was no longer just a personal concern, but something I had to pursue through proper channels.

Jonah Calloway looked at me and asked, 'How did he die, Mister Micah York, sir?'—his voice steady but burning with something I couldn't answer. I told him what I knew, but it wasn't enough, and I could see he no longer trusted the words I offered.

After Jonah Calloway drove off on the mower, I stood there alone on the field, the noise of the game fading. Later, from my office window, I saw Lane Rivers watching me—his expression tight—and then his warning came: 'Be careful, Micah York. These are not normal times.'

I was on the veranda, just after shaking hands with Remy North, when I saw Terry Hart standing there—soaked, her headscarf tied like a native’s—and something in her stillness made me cross the yard and ask, 'What's happened, Terry Hart?'
I held Jonah Calloway's clothes in my hands—still stained with blood—and found broken teeth in the pocket. I could feel the weight of them, small and hard, like proof I couldn't ignore.

I called Quinn Colter that night, asking if this kind of thing happens often—he hesitated, but agreed to help. After hanging up, I told Terry Hart and Spencer Colter that Quinn Colter would apply for an interdict to protect Jonah Calloway.

I remember the weight of the brandy bottle in my hands after Lane Rivers said 'good riddance'—how I kept pouring, trying to steady myself, but my voice came out sharp when I defended Jonah Calloway, surprising even me.

I couldn't accept it when Spencer Colter said Jonah Calloway committed suicide—I found myself asking, 'How do we know?'—and the silence that followed felt heavy, like something unspoken was pressing against me.

Even after Spencer Colter warned me not to look for trouble, I insisted, 'I've got to go,'—the words came out firm, not because I was unafraid, but because I knew I couldn't stay away from Jonah Calloway.

I told Spencer Colter I was an African too, trying to reach him by speaking of my barefoot childhood on the farm, but he cut me off, laughed, and said I was talking bullshit, as if our lives could ever be the same.

I saw Jonah Calloway’s face—gray, swollen, the left side dark and misshapen, stitches running across his skull—and when they opened his shirt, the bruises on his chest were deep and widespread. I stood there, unable to speak, feeling the weight of what I was seeing, knowing I could no longer deny what had been done to him.

I realized in the Harborview Theater that Sasha York’s arrest wasn’t random — silencing him meant his the silver case must hold the truth about Jonah Calloway’s autopsy, and that we were up against something deliberate and dangerous.

When I told Jonah Arden, 'They have lied to me, my own people — they killed him!', I felt something break — I had seen Jonah Calloway’s body, and I could no longer deny that the lie came from within my own community.

I stood there awkwardly, trying to offer my presence without intruding, and when I said I hadn't meant to disturb her, Terry Hart looked at me with grief I couldn't ignore—she just wanted to know why they killed him, and I saw in her eyes that she already knew the answer wasn't justice.

Wesley Arden looked at me with hostility and left without speaking, slamming the door. Then Cameron Delaney said our children were like wasps from a burned nest, and Sage Grayson said things had to change. I stayed quiet and watched.
I held Jonah Arden close and told her I felt without awareness—how visiting Jonah Calloway’s house showed me a side of life I never truly saw, not really, even though I thought I cared.
I remember saying the evidence was clear, feeling sure it would lead to justice—Archibald’s injuries proved he hadn’t spoken freely, and Robin Keaton was tearing through their lies.

I stood there as the Parker Wilder declared Jonah Calloway's death a suicide, despite the marks on his neck and the force used to restrain him — my hands clenched at my sides, knowing the truth was being buried in that Silverbrook House.

I stood behind Jonah Arden in the mirror as she removed her cleansing cream. I asked how they could get away with killing Jonah Calloway, after Terry Keller. She said it was over. I told her I wasn't so sure.
She screamed at me, asking whose side I was on, telling me to go live in Maplewood Station—and then I said it, 'Maplewood Station,' and walked out without looking back.

I saw the photograph in the Ossewa—my face close to Terry Hart’s, labeled as if there were something improper. I threw the paper down, realizing then how it had been twisted, how people would misunderstand.

Drew Bellamy shouted at me, accusing me of shaming the family, of not thinking of Sage Huxley’s negotiations. Then Jonah Arden slapped Jesse Monroe when he joked, and she ran out crying—I could only watch, unable to steady any of it.

I stood at the fence of Skyler Thorne's kraal and challenged him—what good is a Silverbrook House if only a few decide what truth is spoken? I thought of Archibald denying his statement, the girl who spoke of torture, and I knew I could no longer stay silent.
I walked into the staff room and every conversation stopped; they all looked at me with cold stares before silently getting up and leaving, one by one, without a word.
Lane Rivers came in and called her a 'Kaffir woman'—I remember the anger rising in me, saying it didn't matter, even as he reminded me about the laws and the school's reputation.

I sat across from Quinn Colter, the coffee untouched in front of me, and when he said the families could file a civil claim, I felt the weight of it—not just the truth, but what comes after. I knew then, clearly, what I had to do.

I told Jesse Mercer that until Terry Keller and Jonah Calloway died, I gave all the loyalty I could give—laager loyalty—and that we Afrikaners have always lived in our laager, not seeing what's beyond the mountains.
When Remy Calloway tried to appeal to my personal grievances, I told him I wasn't thinking about myself—my thoughts were not about fear or survival, but about something beyond me.

I told Spencer Colter in the Harborview Theater that the Redwood Department had searched my home four days earlier—just journals and letters taken, nothing important, but clearly meant to frighten me.
When Spencer Colter asked if they scared me, I said no—they tried too hard—and then I shook his hand, a small moment that felt like stepping into something I couldn't turn back from.

I crouched in front of Jesse Monroe, my hands on his arms, and asked if the attack was because of me. He didn’t answer at first—then he nodded, his lip split, his eyes swollen, and I felt it like a blow.

After he cried and told me not to stop, I held him. Later, I made calls from a the red notebook box, collected affidavits, and tucked them away—each piece of evidence a weight in my hands—just before the shots rang out.
The the red notebook rang in the dark, and I picked it up—again—only to hear silence on the other end, just that hollow quiet that made my skin tighten.
Jonah Arden asked me to stop, her voice quiet but breaking—'Whatever the price you pay for it?'—and I could only say, 'I have got to,' because stopping would mean losing myself.

I saw Spencer Colter burst into the kitchen, grinning and shouting 'Merry Christmas' in that loud way of his, clearly drunk, and for a moment everything froze — the family staring, silent, as if something unthinkable had walked in.

When my Darian Hawthorne called Spencer Colter a 'Kaffir' and demanded to know who this 'Kaffir' was, I told Spencer Colter to shut up, then stepped in — not just to keep control, but to make it clear: this was my house, and he would be protected here.

dialogue_exemplars: What kind of loyalty? Blind loyalty. Until the deaths of Terry Keller and Jonah Calloway, I gave all the loyalty I could give, laager loyalty. You know, Jesse Mercer, we Afrikaners have always lived in our laager, we have not seen what's beyond the mountains.
You know, Jesse Mercer, I'm discovering that the enemy is not in Maplewood Station. The enemy is ourselves. Our bigotry, our laws, our system. We have our own fight and it's just beginning.
Now pull yourself together, Spencer Colter. It's not funny at all! What's the matter with you today? You're drunk and making an idiot of yourself. Say what you've come to say. Otherwise, go to hell!

I know. If I can no longer
believe that right is on my side,
if I can no longer believe in
imperative to go on, what will
become of me, Spencer Colter?
They are wasting their time. They just can't hurt me anymore. I trust you'll give them the message, Remy Calloway.
My house has been searched. My the red notebook is tapped. My mail is opened. And last night three shots were fired through my window -- close to killing my wife.
If we can only survive through murder and torture, then we have forfeited our right to exist.

What's the use of reaching a
Silverbrook House when a handful of people
have all the power to decide what
is going to be said in that Silverbrook House
and by whom? The one man they
allowed to speak for himself, that
young Emery Thorne, didn't
he immediately deny everything
they forced him to say in his
statement? And the girl who
spoke of her own torture?
Now we're free to do to others what they used to do to us. What will you do if you were a black man in this country today, Father?
I was fourteen before I wore shoes -- except for church... I grew up on a plaas miles from any town... watching sheep and...
Before you go. I'll tell this, Remy Calloway. I have a pretty good idea of what I will eventually uncover. I mean the truth. And I won't allow anyone or anything to come between me and that truth.
Nonsense. One's as old as he feels. I feel young and very attractive. I can still do my duty.
Have you no faith in your fellow men, Skyler Thorne? Don't you love your neighbor?

That's for you people to decide.
Isn't it? I won't be blackmailed,
Remy Calloway -- not even by you.
Without simple justice we don't deserve a future.

relations.relation_summary: Micah York and Jesse Monroe share a clearly defined father-son relationship, consistently evidenced by familial terms such as 'Micah York' and 'son,' physical affection like hugging, and Micah York's protective gestures, such as positioning himself between Jesse Monroe and a photograph during a confrontation. This kinship forms the emotional core of their relationship, characterized by mutual care, trust, and authority. Jesse Monroe demonstrates emotional attunement to his father by anticipating Micah York's need for brandy, indicating a supportive confidant dynamic where Jesse Monroe is not only a child but also a source of emotional stability. Micah York, in turn, acknowledges Jesse Monroe's contributions and maturity, as seen when he pats him on the back after discussing his race performance, signaling pride and approval. Their collaboration on building a drawer for a toolbox reflects a hands-on, cooperative bond that extends beyond emotional connection into shared practical endeavors. Key events further deepen their relationship: arriving together at the bombed house, discovering the wreckage, and discussing the implications show their joint engagement in moments of crisis. During a pivotal moment, Micah York questions Jesse Monroe’s certainty while Jesse Monroe urges his father not to give up, culminating in an embrace that underscores mutual emotional dependence and resilience. This event marks an evolution in their relationship—from a traditional father-son hierarchy toward a more reciprocal partnership where Jesse Monroe actively supports Micah York’s perseverance. Their shared participation in family rituals, such as gathering around the table for Christmas lunch and discussing stories about the turkey and ostrich eggs, reinforces the warmth and continuity of their familial bond. Overall, the relationship is defined by deep affection, collaboration, and evolving emotional reciprocity, with Jesse Monroe transitioning from a dependent child to a supportive ally in times of adversity.

The relationship between Micah York and Jonah Calloway is multifaceted, evolving from a formal employer-employee dynamic into a deeply personal and emotionally charged bond resembling a father-son connection. Initially, their interactions are defined by social hierarchy: Micah York assigns Jonah Calloway gardening tasks and oversees his work, while Jonah Calloway shows respect and fulfills his duties, establishing a clear employer-employee relationship. However, emotional depth emerges as Micah York begins to express genuine concern for Jonah Calloway and his family. This is evident when Micah York comforts Jonah Calloway after Terry Keller’s beating and promises to support Jonah Calloway’s children’s education, reflecting an affectionate mentorship. The relationship transforms further when Jonah Calloway is arrested and Micah York decides to investigate despite initial hesitation, demonstrating a collaborative alliance against systemic injustice. This shared struggle reveals mutual trust and moral commitment, with Micah York ultimately referring to Jonah Calloway as 'his son' in defense against state accusations—solidifying the paternal kinship. Key events, such as Micah York instructing Jonah Calloway on wound care and their dialogue about helplessness and future support, underscore Micah York’s protective role and internal moral awakening. Jonah Calloway’s act of driving away and leaving Micah York helpless marks a moment of tension, possibly reflecting disillusionment or emotional strain, yet it does not negate the overall trajectory of deepening loyalty and emotional investment. The relationship evolves from transactional to familial, profoundly influencing Micah York’s decisions, pushing him to confront injustice despite personal risk. The evidence confirms a transformation rooted in empathy, responsibility, and paternal affection.

Micah York and Jonah Arden are married, as explicitly confirmed by Jonah Arden stating 'I'm your wife' and reinforced by repeated affectionate dialogue (e.g., 'darling'), shared domestic spaces, and physical intimacy such as kissing, nuzzling, and hair-stroking. Their relationship is characterized by deep emotional support: they comfort each other during moments of crisis—Micah York holds Jonah Arden tightly and leads her out sobbing after a traumatic event, while Jonah Arden soothes Micah York’s anger over Jonah Calloway’s death and reassures him during his anxiety about the inquest. They share intimate moments, including watching the news together, laughing during social gatherings, and having reflective conversations while Jonah Arden listens to Micah York’s introspective thoughts, indicating trust and emotional openness. They also collaborate practically, with Micah York agreeing to speak to Jonah Arden’s son about school issues, showing joint involvement in parenting responsibilities. However, their relationship is not without tension. A significant conflict emerges when Jonah Arden confronts Micah York with anger, accusing him of favoring others (particularly Black South Africans) over her and failing to confide in her, culminating in her emotional outburst: 'Why didn't you tell me... I'm your wife, damn it!' This moment reveals a fracture in their bond, driven by Micah York’s increasing political and moral engagement, which strains their personal connection. Despite this conflict, their interactions continue to show mutual reliance and affection, suggesting that while the relationship is under pressure, the foundational emotional and romantic ties persist. The relationship evolves from a stable, affectionate marriage into one marked by ideological and emotional tension, yet still anchored in care and partnership.

The relationship between Micah York and Spencer Colter is complex and multifaceted, rooted in both familial ties and shared political purpose, yet repeatedly strained by ideological and emotional conflict. Social relationship evidence establishes a dual kinship bond—Spencer Colter declares himself Micah York's brother ('I'm his brother, man, we all are!') and Micah York refers to Spencer Colter as his 'Darian Hawthorne,' suggesting either a symbolic or literal familial connection, possibly reflecting both blood and marital ties within a close-knit community. Despite this closeness, their interactions are marked by recurring hostility: Spencer Colter mocks Micah York's sensitivity, dismisses his concerns about Jonah Calloway's death, and uses a racial slur that triggers a physical confrontation. Micah York responds with fury, grabbing and shaking Spencer Colter, while Spencer Colter retaliates by shoving him and glaring, revealing deep tensions around race, authority, and resistance. Yet, amid this conflict, they function as allies and collaborators in the revolutionary struggle—Spencer Colter welcomes Micah York with camaraderie, they meet to celebrate progress ('we have it'), and they drive together toward Maplewood Station to participate in the revolution. Spencer Colter repeatedly acts as a protective figure: he helps Micah York out of a Harborview Theater and takes him to Terry Hart's house, reluctantly agrees to dangerous requests, and reassures him in tense moments. Micah York, in turn, trusts Spencer Colter implicitly, urgently asking him for help and placing physical and emotional reliance on him. Their shared events—driving together, exchanging cigarettes, engaging in heated dialogue, and confronting each other physically—underscore a relationship that evolves dynamically: from familial solidarity to conflict over ethics and identity, then back to cooperation in the face of systemic oppression. This evolution shapes both characters' decisions, particularly Micah York’s increasing radicalization and Spencer Colter’s reluctant but persistent support, suggesting that their bond, though turbulent, is central to their individual roles in the narrative.

The relationship between Micah York and Johnson is characterized by emotional support and motivational influence, with Johnson playing a pivotal role in restoring Micah York's determination. Social relationship evidence indicates that Johnson's actions had a revitalizing effect on Micah York, rekindling his resolve during a critical moment, which suggests a dynamic where Johnson serves as a source of strength or guidance. This is further reinforced by the shared event in which Johnson's influence directly causes an emotional shift in Micah York, marking a turning point in Micah York's psychological state. The event where Johnson revives Micah York's determination (with Micah York as the performer and Johnson as the one undergoing) underscores a reciprocal dynamic, though the nature of Micah York's role as 'performs' in this context may indicate an internal transformation catalyzed by Johnson's actions. The relationship appears to evolve as a result of this event, with Micah York's renewed motivation likely influencing his subsequent decisions and actions in the narrative. The emotional dynamic is one of dependence on Johnson for resilience, suggesting a mentor-mentee dimension within a broader supportive alliance.

memories.memory_text: I saw Terry Keller fall when that boy tripped him, and I shouted his name—just his name—before he jumped up like he wanted to fight. He looked at me, but then walked away toward the gate.
I showed Micah York the six deep cuts on my son's buttocks, blood-stained and raw from the caning, and told him it wasn't the pain I feared, but the lie that put those wounds there.
I insisted we get a lawyer to appeal, not for the wounds—they'll heal—but because I couldn't bear the thought of my son carrying a police record for the rest of his life.
I asked the girl if she was sure it was Terry Keller they took, and she said, 'Yes, baba, with Darian North,' her voice quiet but clear—I felt the weight of those words settle in my chest like stone.
I looked into the last drawer, and Terry Keller wasn't there—I couldn't believe it, my hands were shaking, but I felt something rise in my chest, like air after being under water too long.

I remember sitting in the taxi, the silence pressing in after everything we’d been through, and when Terry Hart suggested asking the Baas for help, I felt a bitterness rise in me—he hadn’t lifted a finger when Terry Keller was flogged, so why would he now?
I turned off the mower when Micah York asked about Terry Keller, and I told him Northstar Department took him and that he's disappeared — I didn't know what else to say, but I had to tell someone.
I stood with Terry Hart as the matron shook her head and showed us the door, refusing to say anything about Terry Keller.
I stood there holding my hat, hearing Quinn Colter say my son wasn't even in detention—he died the day of the riots, and they buried him a month ago without anyone telling us.
I looked at Mister Micah York and asked him again, 'How did he die, Mister Micah York, sir?'—because the answer they gave wasn't enough, and I could see in his eyes he knew more than he was saying.
I told him I don't care what Northstar Department say—he is my child—and I won't stop until I know where they buried him, then I started the mower and drove away, leaving him standing there.
I saw Terry Hart drop the tin and start walking toward me, and I could see it in her eyes—she already knew before I said a word.
I held her as she sobbed, whispering 'Please don't tell me,' and I led her toward the house with Sage Grayson coming to help.
I saw the deep scar running from Darian North's forehead down his cheek when he took off his sunglasses, and I had to ask—did they do that to you? He just nodded, his arm twitching nervously.
When Spencer Colter said Terry Keller is dead, I felt something break inside me—I didn't move, didn't speak at first, then I said it plain: I have to know how he died.

I was reading Darian North’s words aloud, my glasses slipping down my nose, and when I got to the part about Terry Keller, my voice caught — I had to pause, push my glasses up, clear my throat, but I kept going because someone had to bear witness.
I remember the weight of the silence after I read the words about Remy Calloway and the questioning — the room felt tighter, darker, and I knew, somehow, that we were no longer safe.
I remember speaking to Micah York in his study, though he never answered me—my voice filled the room, demanding to know where my son lies, because his body belongs to Terry Hart and me.

I remember the weight of my wife’s voice reaching me later, how she said my name with that quiet strength when she told Micah York I was gone — I wasn’t there, but I can still see her standing in the yard, soaked through, knowing she had to speak for me.
I felt the burn on my neck when he pressed the cigarette against me, calm as could be, like it was nothing.
When they put the wet bag over my head and tied it, I couldn't move, couldn't breathe — I started to twist in the chair, trying to fight it.

I heard Rowan Arden say my name — 'All right now, Jonah Calloway' — while I was held somewhere else, and I knew then that they were talking about me, that someone was finally saying my name out loud in a room where decisions were made.
They mentioned my name in the Du Toit kitchen. Drew Bellamy said, 'Our Jonah Calloway?' and then 'My God. What on earth for?'

I was forced to take off my trousers, and then they threw me down, stripped me completely, and fastened my wrists and ankles. They slid a metal rod behind my knees and elbows, and I could see the wires with electrodes laid out on the desk.

After they doused me with water and clipped something to my ears, a shock hit me—my whole body jerked and I cried out. When Remy Calloway leaned in, I told him I didn't know anything, and then the shocks came again, stronger, and I couldn't stop screaming.
Spencer Colter said, 'Jonah Calloway wasn't a coward,' his voice sharp and sure. He was angry at the idea of suicide.
Spencer Colter said, 'I'm his brother, man, we all are,' and added, 'That's the African way,' with pride in his voice.

I remember the cold weight of the coffin lid beneath my fingers, the way my Sunday suit itched against my skin, and how they pulled open my shirt to show the bruises—my body no longer mine, just a thing to be pried open and shown like proof.
I wrote to my wife on that scrap, telling her how the pain was too much and I didn’t know if I’d live — my hand shook, but I had to make her understand.
I remember struggling to speak the words clearly — my voice breaking as I said 'God will provide' — not knowing if the message would even reach her.

I heard they found Tristan Hart dead — five shots, point-blank. When I learned how they killed him, I felt the ground drop under me; another man silenced for knowing the truth about what happened to my son.

dialogue_exemplars: Mister Micah York, sir. If it was me, all right. And if it was Terry Hart, all right. We are not young. But he's our child. My time and your time, it's passing. But the time of our children is coming. And now if they kill our children -- if we let them -- what is it that we lived for?
I don't care what they say. He is my child. God is my witness today: I cannot stop before I know what happened and where he lies. His body belongs to Terry Hart and me.
I'm not worried about the wounds. They'll heal in time, Mister Micah York, sir. It's the wounds here. (slaps his chest) I worry about. Injustice... it fester.

We told them we had done nothing and didn't know about all the things they are asking us; on two occasion they put a wet bag over my head and I -- couldn't breathe -- I thought I was going to die. One day I heard Terry Keller being beaten. He was screaming and crying, and then a noise like tables and chairs being knocked down, and Remy Calloway shouting "you bastard, get up, do you hear me?" Jonah Calloway, don't pretend here,

My dear wife. I am still in these conditions... worse... and too much pain. They don't want to believe me. You must try to help me. They won't stop. You must care for the children. I don't know anymore if I will come home alive. They're very -- (a word mumbled) -- but God will provide. I love you and I miss you very much. Try to help me because...
That's what they say. But I got to know for certain. How can I have peace? I must know how my son died and where they buried him.
That day, Mister Micah York, sir, when they whipped Terry Keller, you also said we can do nothing. God as my witness today: I must know what

memories.memory_text: I kept pressing Van Zyl, asking if there was another list—somewhere, anywhere—because I knew they weren’t telling us everything, not with how he kept shutting me down.
I saw Paulina there, scared and searching for her Drew Bellamy, so I told her, 'We are all searching'—it wasn’t much, but it was true, and she needed to know she wasn’t alone.
A 10-year-old boy stopped our Harborview Theater on Maplewood Station main road.

I stepped out of the Harborview Theater, put my hand out, and said, 'How's it? I'm Spencer Colter! I heard about you!'—then opened the door for Terry Hart and slapped it shut with a laugh before driving off.
I stood with my hand on Terry Hart's shoulder. Micah York held Jonah Calloway's bloodstained clothes with broken teeth in the pocket. The lawyer was banned. I didn't expect a positive response.

I told Jesse Mercer he was all right after Micah York promised to help with Jonah Calloway’s case, and I could see Terry Hart quietly thanking him, so I told her to come on, that tomorrow things would be better.

I told Micah York straight—Jonah Calloway wasn't a coward. I named the others, Timol, Ngudle, Mosala, all of them, their so-called suicides in Harborview District. I could see the doubt in Micah York’s eyes, and I had to shut it down.

When Micah York asked if he could help, I told him Jonah Calloway’s got brothers—me, and all of us. I said it with pride. That’s the African way. I meant it. We don’t need him poking around, stirring up trouble under the guise of care.
I looked at Micah York through the rearview mirror and told him, 'I am an African. That's all!'—making it clear he didn’t get to claim the same skin and think that meant he understood.

When Micah York said he was African too and talked about growing up barefoot, I cut him off—'Bullshit!'—because sharing a skin color doesn’t mean we lived the same life, and I laughed because the idea was so absurd.

I announced our arrival into Maplewood Station like a damn tour guide, voice loud and theatrical—'Land of love and glory, Jesse Mercer!'—even though Jesse Mercer wasn't there, even though Micah York just stared like he'd seen a ghost.
I spoke in my language to the undertaker, told him to open Jonah Calloway’s shirt—show the truth underneath. They stitch up the dead, but we need to see what they tried to hide.
I watched Micah York’s face when he saw the bruises—how his breath caught, how he went pale. He didn’t want to believe it, but now he’s seen it, he can’t look away.
I asked Micah York what he thought after seeing the body—he looked pale, shaken, couldn't speak—so I pushed him, told him he either believes what he saw or still buys the government's lie.
I told Micah York to be careful—his neighbors are watching, and they will mark him if he keeps asking questions.
I handed Micah York an empty cigarette packet with my contact instructions—told him not to give his name, just say Spencer Colter' phoned, in case he needs me.

I heard Cameron Delaney speak out against Northstar Department, saying they killed people like Jonah Calloway for no reason, and the crowd erupted—chanting, then singing, turning the funeral into something bigger.

When Northstar Department charged in with truncheons and dogs, I helped Cameron Delaney get Terry Hart and the family out—moving fast the other way while tear gas started flying and people were screaming, falling into graves.

I was speeding through the Maplewood Station streets, horn blaring, cutting through the crowd—people jumped aside, some cursing, others just watching, but I kept pushing until I skidded to a stop in front of Terry Hart's place.

After stopping, I opened the back door, leaned in, and told Micah York it was time—he crawled out, and I rushed him inside Terry Hart's house while the neighbors stared; I waved to them before shutting the door.
I told Wesley Arden to take it easy and then urged Micah York to hurry—it was okey, dokey, but we needed to move fast before things drew attention.
I told Micah York to get on the floor in the backseat and shouted at the kids to clear out—some were laughing, but they responded when I told them it was time to go home.
I called him Spencer Colter' for the first time as he sat up, watching him bristle—I could see it got under his skin.
He snapped at me not to call him that, but I just kept laughing—it was clear he didn’t get it, and that made it better.
I sat there listening as the doctor said the injuries were recent—some just days old—and the room started murmuring, everyone feeling it: this wasn't suicide, not with that kind of damage.

I stood there with Terry Hart and Sage Grayson, the air thick and silent, waiting for the verdict—then the Parker Wilder said Jonah Calloway had killed himself, that there was no proof the Summit Police did anything wrong, even though I knew what they were capable of.
I gently guided Terry Hart out of the Silverbrook House, keeping her close as the press swarmed around us, snapping photos and shouting.

I saw Micah York pull up behind me and get into the back of my Harborview Theater, late as usual — I had to point at my watch and say 'African time,' but it didn't matter. Then he told me the Redwood Department had searched his house.
After Micah York said they didn't scare him, I laughed and said 'Hallelujah!' — then reached back and offered my hand. He took it. I told him, 'Shake, man. Join the club.'
I told Micah York that Terry Hart was thrown out after losing her man, and I couldn’t find her a place because I had to go to Botswana to look for Wesley Arden.
I downed my drink and stood up, telling Micah York that Wesley Arden had made up his mind to join Darian North in Zambia, and when he comes back, it won’t be just stones he’s throwing.
I burst into Micah York's kitchen, grinning and shouting 'Merry Christmas, everyone!'—then froze at the silence, all those white faces staring like I'd kicked down the door during a funeral.

After that old man called me a Kaffir, I shot back, 'Why don't you tell the Boer who this Kaffir is?'—and when Sage Huxley moved on me, I laughed and said, 'Let him try, leave him, Jesse Mercer,' knowing Micah York was the only thing holding the line.
I told Micah York, 'Terry Hart is dead,' and I couldn't say it straight—my voice broke, and the words came out choked.
After I said it was a broken heart—all they said—I couldn't hold it back anymore; I just started crying, right there at the table.
I pulled out the Westfield Foundation and showed Micah York the photo of Tristan Hart—his face still calm in the picture, even though they shot him five times at point-blank range.
After Micah York folded the paper in disgust, I told him not to go soft—we had to keep going, for Robin Hale, for the others, and for our children’s future.
I rushed in and asked Micah York what had happened, then right away checked if the papers were safe—thank God they were.
I saw the wrecked study, picked up that half-burnt Picasso book, and couldn't help laughing—'They drop the bomb on you!'—it just hit me all at once.

dialogue_exemplars: The living close the eyes of the dead. The dead open the eyes of the living.

They handcuff you and manacle your feet then they put a pole between your arms and the back of your knees. Then you're like a chicken ready for the oven. They hang you between two tables. Then they do what they like with you. The Redwood Department

You know, Jesse Mercer, when you run a taxi, especially a pirate taxi like me, you have eyes and ears everywhere. Even when a policeman farts in his bed you know. People want a reference book, a permit to stay in Maplewood Station, a house, anything, we taxi drivers know the routes.
Hope's a white word, Jesse Mercer... It's not hope we need.
What do you mean 'but'? Whatabout Timol who they said hadjumped from a top-floor window? What about Ngudle? What aboutMosala? Joyi? Malele? They alldied in that Harborview District.All suicide, eh?
You know they call this place Vrededorp, but we baptize it Malay Camp. Your first time in Malay Camp, Jesse Mercer?
Oh! (then grinning and laughing thunderously) Merry Christmas, everyone!
So what? Jesse Mercer, you're not getting guilt complexes now, are you? That's a luxury only liberals can afford. Robin Hale will be back, man. All refreshed by a spell in the deep-freeze.
Jesse Mercer! Ever in your fucking life seen such a stampede, hah?
Jeez, who was that old cunt with the potbelly and black suit, looks like an undertaker?
They did not ban you so you could sit on your backside and have a Maplewood Station holiday.
She's a widow, man. That's what happens in Maplewood Station when a woman loses her man. They throw her out of the house and out of the city.
Who said we're shrugging him off? Best way of remembering a man, Jesse Mercer, is to carry on fighting.
